title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Creating numeric vectors (quickly)
:: create a sequence from the left to the right number, separated by 1.
seq(): creates a sequence from a number to a number by and interval.
rep(): replicates a vector times times.

4:8

[1] 4 5 6 7 8

seq(from = 1, to = 3, by = .1)

 [1] 1.0 1.1 1.2 1.3 1.4 1.5 1.6 1.7 1.8 1.9 2.0 2.1 2.2 2.3 2.4 2.5 2.6 2.7 2.8
[20] 2.9 3.0

seq(1, 3, .1)

 [1] 1.0 1.1 1.2 1.3 1.4 1.5 1.6 1.7 1.8 1.9 2.0 2.1 2.2 2.3 2.4 2.5 2.6 2.7 2.8
[20] 2.9 3.0

rep(1:3, times = 2)

[1] 1 2 3 1 2 3

# What three commands will generate the following vectors?
# [1] 5.0 5.5 6.0 6.5 7.0
# [1]  2  1  0 -1 -2
# [1] "cat"   "dog"   "dingo" "cat"   "dog"   "dingo"


seq(from = 5, to = 7, by = .5)

[1] 5.0 5.5 6.0 6.5 7.0

seq(from = 2, to = -2, by = -1)

[1]  2  1  0 -1 -2

2:-2 # also works!

[1]  2  1  0 -1 -2

rep(char_vec, times = 2)

[1] "cat"   "dog"   "dingo" "cat"   "dog"   "dingo"

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Behavior of Vectors
Vectorization: Operations and functions that can run on an entire vector at once.
Vector Recycling: If a function requires a longer vector than provided, it will fill with the existing elements, in order.

c(2, 6, 1)^2

[1]  4 36  1

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Type Coersion
Implicit Coersion: Conversion of data types to ensure atomic vectors according to a hierarchy.
Logical < Integer < Double < Character

c(TRUE, FALSE, 3)

[1] 1 0 3

mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))

[1] 0.3333333


Note: logical vectors can be coerced to integers for mathematical operations
Explicit Coersion
as.__(x): sets x to be of type ___

distances <- c("2800", "450", "10")
distances

[1] "2800" "450"  "10"  

mean(distances)

Warning in mean.default(distances): argument is not numeric or logical:
returning NA


[1] NA

distances <- as.double(distances)
distances

[1] 2800  450   10

mean(distances)

[1] 1086.667

title: Explanatory Data Analysis
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)


Features

consumer: the analyst
goal: uncover structure for further analysis
follow templates
prioritize quick and accurate interpretation


Common Exploratory Questions

What is the unit of observation?
What are the variables, their types, and levels?
How is missingness encoded? How prevalent is it?
What is the distribution of the variables?
Are there any interesting outliers?
Use View() in Positron

title: Explanatory Data Analysis
text:
Explanatory Data Analysis


Features

consumer: stakeholder
goal: tell a specific story
customized
polished aesthetic


Common Exploratory Questions

Who is my audience?
What is the main story?
How can I facilitate comparisons?
Can my plot be clearly read?
Is it polished and customized for audience?

Following a similar structure to the lecture, you will perform an elemenary exploratory analysis of a work of your choosing cataloged by Project Gutenberg (https://www.gutenberg.org/). Read the data into R.

title: STAT 133
text:
Using the notions of durations, periods, and timezones from lubridate, provide the code and output to answer the following questions.

How old are you? Answer as a duration.









How old will you be in one month? Answer both using durations and periods.








What time is it now? Answer using the now() function in lubridate and answer in HH:MM:SS and provide the timezone.






What is the current time in UTC (that is to say, in London)?






Now imagine you call your friend right now in Delhi, India and ask them to do the same on their phone. What will they say? (in HH:MM:SS with timezone).






These exercises will be easiest done iteratively in R. You can copy your answers back here or produce your problem set document using Quarto directly. The data set at hand is called flights inside the nycflights package.

library(lubridate)    # this is also in library(tidyverse)

Start by reading the documention for the data frame. What is the unit of observation? What time span and geography is covered by this data? Which time zones are any time columns recorded in?







Using year, month, day, and the integer clock times sched_dep_time and dep_time (HHMM)1, add two more variables to your data frame:


sched_dep_ts: the scheduled departure timestamp.

dep_ts: the actual wheels-off timestamp

Both must be POSIXct in the “America/New_York” time zone.








Calculate the actual wheels-off timestamp in two additional ways and store them as additional variables in your data frame:


dep_ts_dur: add to sched_dep_ts the recorded time span of the departure delay as a duration.
dep_ts_per: add to sched_dep_ts the recorded time span of the departure delay as a period.

In general do the different approaches align? How about if you look at the precise edge of a switch to/from Daylight Savings Time?






Challenge: Construct scheduled and realized arrival timestamps using only columns in flights. Build sched_arr_ts from year, month, day, and sched_arr_time (HHMM) in “America/New_York”.

For red-eyes that arrive after midnight local time, sched_arr_time may be smaller than sched_dep_time. Correct the date by adding a day to sched_arr_ts when needed.
Do the analogous construction for actual arr_ts from arr_time.
Then compute:

sched_block = as.duration(sched_arr_ts - sched_dep_ts)
actual_block = as.duration(arr_ts - dep_ts)

Report the median difference actual_block - sched_block in minutes.

title: Strings I
text:
Escape Characters
You can change the default meaning of a given character by escaping it: prepending it with \.

" normally starts or ends a string. \" is the double-quote character.
t normally is the lowercase Latin t. \t is a tab space.
n normally is the lowercase Latin n. \n is a new line.
U0001F600 normal is just that. \U0001F600 is 😀.

Each of the following questions should be answered using the storms data set built into dplyr. Provide the code to construct each of the following plots and make a sketch of the resulting plot. No need to enumerate all of the detail of the data in the plot but focus on the general shape and be sure to be clear what all axes and legends are (i.e. what the aesthetic mappings are).

Plot the distribution of the wind speed three ways: as a histogram, a box plot, and a density curve.












A bar chart showing the distribution of storm status found across all records in the data set.














A bar chart showing the distribution of storm status of when considering just one record for each named storm1.













A scatterplot of the relationship between wind speed and pressure for every record in the data set.

A line plot of the relationship between wind speed and pressure for all of the storms in 2014. Each storm should be indicated with a different color2.











Create a line plot that shows the average duration of storms over time. That is: the x-axis should be the year and the y-axis should be average storm duration.

A data frame with the overall mean hours of AI use. Name that statistic mean_ai.

Skim the documentation for the tibble package (https://tibble.tidyverse.org/) then write down three ways in which tibbles behave differently than data frames.

Sampson’s Monks Project: Background Concepts

Packages in R
Sociomatrices
Network visualizations & statistics
Random vs. observed networks


Motivate for students that we will be working on the project and turning it in in 2 weeks, and it will be about the monks data. These are some of the necessary skills they will need for the project

title: Lab 2
text:
Packages & Libraries

Base R is powerful, but we use packages to extend its capabilities
Packages collections of functions & datasets

library() is used to load a previously installed package into an R session.

Install and load:
install.packages("igraph") # only need to do once!
library(igraph)

title: Lab 2
text:
Packages to use today:
igraph (network analysis & static plots)

accepts adjacency matrices.

networkD3 (interactive plots)

expects data frames of nodes and edges, not a network object.
nodes are the names/points in the resulting plot
edges are the directed lines between the points

Even though the information is already in sampson, you still need to extract it into the right format for networkD3.

title: Lab 2
text:
What do networks look like?

Let’s use a familar dataset to create network plots!

title: Lab 2
text:
Our Dataset: Sampson’s Monks

Data collected in a New England monastery (1960s)
Monks reported:

Liking relationships (time 1, time 2, time 3)
Disliking relationships (time 1)

Classic dataset for studying group dynamics and conflict
Stored as a list of matrices in lda package, which we will use to get the data

title: Lab 2
text:
Our Dataset: Sampson’s Monks (continued)
From this matrix, we can get:

In-degree (col sums) = number of ties received / how many monks said they liked them
Out-degree (row sums) = number of ties sent / how many monks they said they liked

title: Lab 2
text:
Static vs. Interactive Plots

You will create one of each in your project
Static plots = easy and quick to create using plot() from igraph
Interactive plots = can zoom, hover, drag nodes using forceNetwork() from networkD3

title: Lab 2
text:
Why Compare Random vs. Observed?
In your project, you will be asked to compare the observed sociomatrix with one that you have generated.

Random sociomatrix = ties assigned by chance
Observed monk network = structured by social dynamics
Key question: What features do we see in the real network that random ones lack?

Shows the complexity of real social systems

Quarto
Quarto is an open-source scientific publishing system that you can run at the command line.

Source document is .qmd and output document can be a pdf, a webpage, slides, a dashboard, etc.
The source document can hold text, images, videos, and code.
Rendering the source document runs all the code and puts the data products into the output document.
$ quarto render mydoc.qmd
Microsoft Word + Microsoft Excel + a lot more.

Shell, R, Editor, Viewer, git, and Quarto all in one place
Successor to RStudio
R, Python, and Julia are equal citizens

Communicate findings clearly to Dr. Bayes.

EV Power Project Overview

Electric vehicles reduce direct emissions, but does the electricity used to charge them actually come from clean sources? How clean is the power that charges America’s EVs, and how does this vary across states?

title: EV Power Project
text:
Let’s Try it Ourseleves:

Dataset: Multiple tables covering U.S. electricity generation by source and average energy costs (2021–2023) from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and US Department of Energy
Goal: Analyze the relationship between EV adoption and the cleanliness of each state’s energy mix to understand how “green” electric driving really is across the US using maps
Client: The everyday consumer wanting to make informed, sustainable choices

title: EV Power Project
text:
Defining Key Terms
Direct emissions:

Greenhouse gases released directly from a vehicle’s operation (exhaust from fuel combustion)

Clean energy:

Produces little to no greenhouse gases (includes nuclear, hydro, wind, solar)

Renewable energy:

Comes from naturally replenished sources like solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass

Join Type

Result




left_join()
Keep all rows from the X table
All X + matching Y


right_join()
Keep all rows from the Y table
All Y + matching X


inner_join()
Keep only matching rows from both
Matching only


full_join()
Keep all rows from both tables
All data combined


semi_join()
Keep rows from X that have matches in Y
X (filtered)


anti_join()
Keep rows from X without matches in Y

slice()
select()
filter()
mutate()
arrange()
summarize()
group_by()



All of these have a data frame as the first argument.

title: Factors and Data Frames
text:
Factors
A data structure for storing categorical data. Stores the values in an integer vector and adds a levels attribute to map integers to character strings. Created with factor().


maj <- factor(x = c("STAT", "ECON", "STAT", "DATA", "ECON"))
maj



[1] STAT ECON STAT DATA ECON
Levels: DATA ECON STAT



Draw two vection of the same data: as a character vector as as an integer vector coupled with a levels lookup table.

title: Factors and Data Frames
text:
as.integer(maj)



[1] 3 2 3 1 2





c(maj, 2L)



[1] 3 2 3 1 2 2

title: Factors and Data Frames
text:
Attributes
Objects built on top of simpler data structures can have attributes. A factor’s attributes include its class and levels.


class(maj)



[1] "factor"





levels(maj)



[1] "DATA" "ECON" "STAT"

title: Factors and Data Frames
text:
Setting Levels
Quickly change all of the values with a particular level.


levels(maj) <- c("DATA", "ECON", "STATISTICS")
maj



[1] STATISTICS ECON       STATISTICS DATA       ECON      
Levels: DATA ECON STATISTICS




Add a level even if it’s not observed.



levels(maj) <- c("DATA", "ECON", "STATISTICS", "BIO")
maj



[1] STATISTICS ECON       STATISTICS DATA       ECON      
Levels: DATA ECON STATISTICS BIO

maj_or <- factor(x = c("STAT", "ECON", "STAT", "DATA", "ECON"),
                 levels = c("STAT", "ECON", "DATA", "BIO"),

Daylight savings time!

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Please answer the following two questions. I will call on someone randomly after the timer is up.

How long is a day?
How long is a year?


This is a revisit of the opening question.
Point out that actually “days” don’t have a single fixed length. Most days are 24 hours but at the edge of daylight savings time, its shorter or longer. Same with leap years. So if you talk about the average day or year length, it’s not quite 24 hrs or 365 days.

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Periods
In lubridate, a period is like a duration except it doesn’t have a fixed length in seconds. It tracks human units (day, week) that are responsive to irregularities.
Example period constructors:



seconds(15)

[1] "15S"

minutes(10)

[1] "10M 0S"

hours(c(12, 24))

[1] "12H 0M 0S" "24H 0M 0S"




days(0:3)

[1] "0S"          "1d 0H 0M 0S" "2d 0H 0M 0S" "3d 0H 0M 0S"

weeks(3)

[1] "21d 0H 0M 0S"

years(1)

[1] "1y 0m 0d 0H 0M 0S"

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Working with periods


one_am



[1] "2026-03-08 01:00:00 EST"





one_am + days(1)



[1] "2026-03-09 01:00:00 EDT"




What will the following yield?

ymd("2024-01-01") + dyears(1)



[1] "2024-12-31 06:00:00 UTC"





ymd("2024-01-01") + years(1) # accounts for leap year



[1] "2025-01-01"

[1] "43y 0m 239d 12H 0M 0S"

 [122] "CHORUS."                                                                              
 [123] "Two households, both alike in dignity,"                                               
 [124] "In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,"                                              
 [125] "From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,"                                             
 [126] "Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean."                                         
 [127] "From forth the fatal loins of these two foes"                                         
 [128] "A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life;"                                       
 [129] "Whose misadventur’d piteous overthrows"                                               
 [130] "Doth with their death bury their parents’ strife."                                    
 [131] "The fearful passage of their death-mark’d love,"                                      
 [132] "And the continuance of their parents’ rage,"                                          
 [133] "Which, but their children’s end, nought could remove,"                                
 [134] "Is now the two hours’ traffic of our stage;"                                          
 [135] "The which, if you with patient ears attend,"                                          
 [136] "What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend."                                 
 [137] ""                                                                                     
 [138] " [_Exit._]"                                                                           
 [139] ""                                                                                     
 [140] ""                                                                                     
 [141] ""                                                                                     
 [142] ""                                                                                     
 [143] "ACT I"                                                                                
 [144] ""                                                                                     
 [145] "SCENE I. A public place."                                                             
 [146] ""                                                                                     
 [147] ""                                                                                     
 [148] " Enter Sampson and Gregory armed with swords and bucklers."                           
 [149] ""                                                                                     
 [150] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [151] "Gregory, on my word, we’ll not carry coals."                                          
 [152] ""                                                                                     
 [153] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [154] "No, for then we should be colliers."                                                  
 [155] ""                                                                                     
 [156] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [157] "I mean, if we be in choler, we’ll draw."                                              
 [158] ""                                                                                     
 [159] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [160] "Ay, while you live, draw your neck out o’ the collar."                                
 [161] ""                                                                                     
 [162] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [163] "I strike quickly, being moved."                                                       
 [164] ""                                                                                     
 [165] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [166] "But thou art not quickly moved to strike."                                            
 [167] ""                                                                                     
 [168] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [169] "A dog of the house of Montague moves me."                                             
 [170] ""                                                                                     
 [171] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [172] "To move is to stir; and to be valiant is to stand: therefore, if thou"                
 [173] "art moved, thou runn’st away."                                                        
 [174] ""                                                                                     
 [175] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [176] "A dog of that house shall move me to stand."                                          
 [177] "I will take the wall of any man or maid of Montague’s."                               
 [178] ""                                                                                     
 [179] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [180] "That shows thee a weak slave, for the weakest goes to the wall."                      
 [181] ""                                                                                     
 [182] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [183] "True, and therefore women, being the weaker vessels, are ever thrust to"              
 [184] "the wall: therefore I will push Montague’s men from the wall, and"                    
 [185] "thrust his maids to the wall."                                                        
 [186] ""                                                                                     
 [187] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [188] "The quarrel is between our masters and us their men."                                 
 [189] ""                                                                                     
 [190] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [191] "’Tis all one, I will show myself a tyrant: when I have fought with the"               
 [192] "men I will be civil with the maids, I will cut off their heads."                      
 [193] ""                                                                                     
 [194] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [195] "The heads of the maids?"                                                              
 [196] ""                                                                                     
 [197] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [198] "Ay, the heads of the maids, or their maidenheads; take it in what sense"              
 [199] "thou wilt."                                                                           
 [200] ""                                                                                     
 [201] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [202] "They must take it in sense that feel it."                                             
 [203] ""                                                                                     
 [204] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [205] "Me they shall feel while I am able to stand: and ’tis known I am a"                   
 [206] "pretty piece of flesh."                                                               
 [207] ""                                                                                     
 [208] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [209] "’Tis well thou art not fish; if thou hadst, thou hadst been poor John."               
 [210] "Draw thy tool; here comes of the house of Montagues."                                 
 [211] ""                                                                                     
 [212] " Enter Abram and Balthasar."                                                          
 [213] ""                                                                                     
 [214] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [215] "My naked weapon is out: quarrel, I will back thee."                                   
 [216] ""                                                                                     
 [217] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [218] "How? Turn thy back and run?"                                                          
 [219] ""                                                                                     
 [220] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [221] "Fear me not."                                                                         
 [222] ""                                                                                     
 [223] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [224] "No, marry; I fear thee!"                                                              
 [225] ""                                                                                     
 [226] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [227] "Let us take the law of our sides; let them begin."                                    
 [228] ""                                                                                     
 [229] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [230] "I will frown as I pass by, and let them take it as they list."                        
 [231] ""                                                                                     
 [232] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [233] "Nay, as they dare. I will bite my thumb at them, which is disgrace to"                
 [234] "them if they bear it."                                                                
 [235] ""                                                                                     
 [236] "ABRAM."                                                                               
 [237] "Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?"                                                   
 [238] ""                                                                                     
 [239] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [240] "I do bite my thumb, sir."                                                             
 [241] ""                                                                                     
 [242] "ABRAM."                                                                               
 [243] "Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?"                                                   
 [244] ""                                                                                     
 [245] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [246] "Is the law of our side if I say ay?"                                                  
 [247] ""                                                                                     
 [248] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [249] "No."                                                                                  
 [250] ""                                                                                     
 [251] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [252] "No sir, I do not bite my thumb at you, sir; but I bite my thumb, sir."                
 [253] ""                                                                                     
 [254] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [255] "Do you quarrel, sir?"                                                                 
 [256] ""                                                                                     
 [257] "ABRAM."                                                                               
 [258] "Quarrel, sir? No, sir."                                                               
 [259] ""                                                                                     
 [260] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [261] "But if you do, sir, I am for you. I serve as good a man as you."                      
 [262] ""                                                                                     
 [263] "ABRAM."                                                                               
 [264] "No better."                                                                           
 [265] ""                                                                                     
 [266] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [267] "Well, sir."                                                                           
 [268] ""                                                                                     
 [269] " Enter Benvolio."                                                                     
 [270] ""                                                                                     
 [271] "GREGORY."                                                                             
 [272] "Say better; here comes one of my master’s kinsmen."                                   
 [273] ""                                                                                     
 [274] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [275] "Yes, better, sir."                                                                    
 [276] ""                                                                                     
 [277] "ABRAM."                                                                               
 [278] "You lie."                                                                             
 [279] ""                                                                                     
 [280] "SAMPSON."                                                                             
 [281] "Draw, if you be men. Gregory, remember thy washing blow."                             
 [282] ""                                                                                     
 [283] " [_They fight._]"                                                                     
 [284] ""                                                                                     
 [285] "BENVOLIO."                                                                            
 [286] "Part, fools! put up your swords, you know not what you do."                           
 [287] ""                                                                                     
 [288] " [_Beats down their swords._]"                                                        
 [289] ""                                                                                     
 [290] " Enter Tybalt."                                                                       
 [291] ""                                                                                     
 [292] "TYBALT."                                                                              
 [293] "What, art thou drawn among these heartless hinds?"                                    
 [294] "Turn thee Benvolio, look upon thy death."                                             
 [295] ""                                                                                     
 [296] "BENVOLIO."                                                                            
 [297] "I do but keep the peace, put up thy sword,"                                           
 [298] "Or manage it to part these men with me."                                              
 [299] ""                                                                                     
 [300] "TYBALT."                                                                              
 [301] "What, drawn, and talk of peace? I hate the word"                                      
 [302] "As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee:"                                             
 [303] "Have at thee, coward."                                                                
 [304] ""                                                                                     
 [305] " [_They fight._]"                                                                     
 [306] ""                                                                                     
 [307] " Enter three or four Citizens with clubs."                                            
 [308] ""                                                                                     
 [309] "FIRST CITIZEN."                                                                       
 [310] "Clubs, bills and partisans! Strike! Beat them down!"                                  
 [311] "Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!"                                     
 [312] ""                                                                                     
 [313] " Enter Capulet in his gown, and Lady Capulet."                                        
 [314] ""                                                                                     
 [315] "CAPULET."                                                                             
 [316] "What noise is this? Give me my long sword, ho!"                                       
 [317] ""                                                                                     
 [318] "LADY CAPULET."                                                                        
 [319] "A crutch, a crutch! Why call you for a sword?"                                        
 [320] ""                                                                                     
 [321] "CAPULET."                                                                             
 [322] "My sword, I say! Old Montague is come,"                                               
 [323] "And flourishes his blade in spite of me."                                             
 [324] ""                                                                                     
 [325] " Enter Montague and his Lady Montague."                                               
 [326] ""                                                                                     
 [327] "MONTAGUE."                                                                            
 [328] "Thou villain Capulet! Hold me not, let me go."                                        
 [329] ""                                                                                     
 [330] "LADY MONTAGUE."                                                                       
 [331] "Thou shalt not stir one foot to seek a foe."                                          
 [332] ""                                                                                     
 [333] " Enter Prince Escalus, with Attendants."                                              
 [334] ""                                                                                     
 [335] "PRINCE."                                                                              
 [336] "Rebellious subjects, enemies to peace,"                                               
 [337] "Profaners of this neighbour-stained steel,—"                                          
 [338] "Will they not hear? What, ho! You men, you beasts,"                                   
 [339] "That quench the fire of your pernicious rage"                                         
 [340] "With purple fountains issuing from your veins,"                                       
 [341] "On pain of torture, from those bloody hands"                                          
 [342] "Throw your mistemper’d weapons to the ground"                                         
 [343] "And hear the sentence of your moved prince."                                          
 [344] "Three civil brawls, bred of an airy word,"                                            
 [345] "By thee, old Capulet, and Montague,"                                                  
 [346] "Have thrice disturb’d the quiet of our streets,"                                      
 [347] "And made Verona’s ancient citizens"                                                   
 [348] "Cast by their grave beseeming ornaments,"                                             
 [349] "To wield old partisans, in hands as old,"                                             
 [350] "Canker’d with peace, to part your canker’d hate."                                     
 [351] "If ever you disturb our streets again,"                                               
 [352] "Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace."                                       
 [353] "For this time all the rest depart away:"                                              
 [354] "You, Capulet, shall go along with me,"                                                
 [355] "And Montague, come you this afternoon,"                                               
 [356] "To know our farther pleasure in this case,"                                           
 [357] "To old Free-town, our common judgement-place."                                        
 [358] "Once more, on pain of death, all men depart."                                         
 [359] ""                                                                                     
 [360] " [_Exeunt Prince and Attendants; Capulet, Lady Capulet, Tybalt,"                      
 [361] " Citizens and Servants._]"                                                            
 [362] ""                                                                                     
 [363] "MONTAGUE."                                                                            
 [364] "Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach?"                                            
 [365] "Speak, nephew, were you by when it began?"                                            
 [366] ""                                                                                     
 [367] "BENVOLIO."                                                                            
 [368] "Here were the servants of your adversary"                                             
 [369] "And yours, close fighting ere I did approach."                                        
 [370] "I drew to part them, in the instant came"                                             
 [371] "The fiery Tybalt, with his sword prepar’d,"                                           
 [372] "Which, as he breath’d defiance to my ears,"                                           
 [373] "He swung about his head, and cut the winds,"                                          
 [374] "Who nothing hurt withal, hiss’d him in scorn."                                        
 [375] "While we were interchanging thrusts and blows"                                        
 [376] "Came more and more, and fought on part and part,"                                     
 [377] "Till the Prince came, who parted either part."                                        
 [378] ""                                                                                     
 [379] "LADY MONTAGUE."                                                                       
 [380] "O where is Romeo, saw you him today?"                                                 
 [381] "Right glad I am he was not at this fray."                                             
 [382] ""                                                                                     
 [383] "BENVOLIO."                                                                            
 [384] "Madam, an hour before the worshipp’d sun"                                             
 [385] "Peer’d forth the golden window of the east,"                                          
 [386] "A troubled mind drave me to walk abroad,"                                             
 [387] "Where underneath the grove of sycamore"                                               
 [388] "That westward rooteth from this city side,"                                           
 [389] "So early walking did I see your son."                                                 
 [390] "Towards him I made, but he was ware of me,"                                           
 [391] "And stole into the covert of the wood."                                               
 [392] "I, measuring his affections by my own,"                                               
 [393] "Which then most sought where most might not be found,"                                
 [394] "Being one too many by my weary self,"                                                 
 [395] "Pursu’d my humour, not pursuing his,"                                                 
 [396] "And gladly shunn’d who gladly fled from me."                                          
 [397] ""                                                                                     
 [398] "MONTAGUE."                                                                            
 [399] "Many a morning hath he there been seen,"                                              
 [400] "With tears augmenting the fresh morning’s dew,"                                       
 [401] "Adding to clouds more clouds with his deep sighs;"                                    
 [402] "But all so soon as the all-cheering sun"                                              
 [403] "Should in the farthest east begin to draw"                                            
 [404] "The shady curtains from Aurora’s bed,"                                                
 [405] "Away from light steals home my heavy son,"                                            
 [406] "And private in his chamber pens himself,"                                             
 [407] "Shuts up his windows, locks fair daylight out"                                        
 [408] "And makes himself an artificial night."                                               
 [409] "Black and portentous must this humour prove,"                                         
 [410] "Unless good counsel may the cause remove."                                            
 [411] ""                                                                                     
 [412] "BENVOLIO."                                                                            
 [413] "My noble uncle, do you know the cause?"                                               
 [414] ""

[5059] "[_Within._] Lead, boy. Which way?"                                                    
[5060] ""                                                                                     
[5061] "JULIET."                                                                              
[5062] "Yea, noise? Then I’ll be brief. O happy dagger."                                      
[5063] ""                                                                                     
[5064] " [_Snatching Romeo’s dagger._]"                                                       
[5065] ""                                                                                     
[5066] "This is thy sheath. [_stabs herself_] There rest, and let me die."                    
[5067] ""                                                                                     
[5068] " [_Falls on Romeo’s body and dies._]"                                                 
[5069] ""                                                                                     
[5070] " Enter Watch with the Page of Paris."                                                 
[5071] ""                                                                                     
[5072] "PAGE."                                                                                
[5073] "This is the place. There, where the torch doth burn."                                 
[5074] ""                                                                                     
[5075] "FIRST WATCH."                                                                         
[5076] "The ground is bloody. Search about the churchyard."                                   
[5077] "Go, some of you, whoe’er you find attach."                                            
[5078] ""                                                                                     
[5079] " [_Exeunt some of the Watch._]"                                                       
[5080] ""                                                                                     
[5081] "Pitiful sight! Here lies the County slain,"                                           
[5082] "And Juliet bleeding, warm, and newly dead,"                                           
[5083] "Who here hath lain this two days buried."                                             
[5084] "Go tell the Prince; run to the Capulets."                                             
[5085] "Raise up the Montagues, some others search."                                          
[5086] ""                                                                                     
[5087] " [_Exeunt others of the Watch._]"                                                     
[5088] ""                                                                                     
[5089] "We see the ground whereon these woes do lie,"                                         
[5090] "But the true ground of all these piteous woes"                                        
[5091] "We cannot without circumstance descry."                                               
[5092] ""                                                                                     
[5093] " Re-enter some of the Watch with Balthasar."                                          
[5094] ""                                                                                     
[5095] "SECOND WATCH."                                                                        
[5096] "Here’s Romeo’s man. We found him in the churchyard."                                  
[5097] ""                                                                                     
[5098] "FIRST WATCH."                                                                         
[5099] "Hold him in safety till the Prince come hither."                                      
[5100] ""                                                                                     
[5101] " Re-enter others of the Watch with Friar Lawrence."                                   
[5102] ""                                                                                     
[5103] "THIRD WATCH. Here is a Friar that trembles, sighs, and weeps."                        
[5104] "We took this mattock and this spade from him"                                         
[5105] "As he was coming from this churchyard side."                                          
[5106] ""                                                                                     
[5107] "FIRST WATCH."                                                                         
[5108] "A great suspicion. Stay the Friar too."                                               
[5109] ""                                                                                     
[5110] " Enter the Prince and Attendants."                                                    
[5111] ""                                                                                     
[5112] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5113] "What misadventure is so early up,"                                                    
[5114] "That calls our person from our morning’s rest?"                                       
[5115] ""                                                                                     
[5116] " Enter Capulet, Lady Capulet and others."                                             
[5117] ""                                                                                     
[5118] "CAPULET."                                                                             
[5119] "What should it be that they so shriek abroad?"                                        
[5120] ""                                                                                     
[5121] "LADY CAPULET."                                                                        
[5122] "O the people in the street cry Romeo,"                                                
[5123] "Some Juliet, and some Paris, and all run"                                             
[5124] "With open outcry toward our monument."                                                
[5125] ""                                                                                     
[5126] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5127] "What fear is this which startles in our ears?"                                        
[5128] ""                                                                                     
[5129] "FIRST WATCH."                                                                         
[5130] "Sovereign, here lies the County Paris slain,"                                         
[5131] "And Romeo dead, and Juliet, dead before,"                                             
[5132] "Warm and new kill’d."                                                                 
[5133] ""                                                                                     
[5134] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5135] "Search, seek, and know how this foul murder comes."                                   
[5136] ""                                                                                     
[5137] "FIRST WATCH."                                                                         
[5138] "Here is a Friar, and slaughter’d Romeo’s man,"                                        
[5139] "With instruments upon them fit to open"                                               
[5140] "These dead men’s tombs."                                                              
[5141] ""                                                                                     
[5142] "CAPULET."                                                                             
[5143] "O heaven! O wife, look how our daughter bleeds!"                                      
[5144] "This dagger hath mista’en, for lo, his house"                                         
[5145] "Is empty on the back of Montague,"                                                    
[5146] "And it mis-sheathed in my daughter’s bosom."                                          
[5147] ""                                                                                     
[5148] "LADY CAPULET."                                                                        
[5149] "O me! This sight of death is as a bell"                                               
[5150] "That warns my old age to a sepulchre."                                                
[5151] ""                                                                                     
[5152] " Enter Montague and others."                                                          
[5153] ""                                                                                     
[5154] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5155] "Come, Montague, for thou art early up,"                                               
[5156] "To see thy son and heir more early down."                                             
[5157] ""                                                                                     
[5158] "MONTAGUE."                                                                            
[5159] "Alas, my liege, my wife is dead tonight."                                             
[5160] "Grief of my son’s exile hath stopp’d her breath."                                     
[5161] "What further woe conspires against mine age?"                                         
[5162] ""                                                                                     
[5163] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5164] "Look, and thou shalt see."                                                            
[5165] ""                                                                                     
[5166] "MONTAGUE."                                                                            
[5167] "O thou untaught! What manners is in this,"                                            
[5168] "To press before thy father to a grave?"                                               
[5169] ""                                                                                     
[5170] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5171] "Seal up the mouth of outrage for a while,"                                            
[5172] "Till we can clear these ambiguities,"                                                 
[5173] "And know their spring, their head, their true descent,"                               
[5174] "And then will I be general of your woes,"                                             
[5175] "And lead you even to death. Meantime forbear,"                                        
[5176] "And let mischance be slave to patience."                                              
[5177] "Bring forth the parties of suspicion."                                                
[5178] ""                                                                                     
[5179] "FRIAR LAWRENCE."                                                                      
[5180] "I am the greatest, able to do least,"                                                 
[5181] "Yet most suspected, as the time and place"                                            
[5182] "Doth make against me, of this direful murder."                                        
[5183] "And here I stand, both to impeach and purge"                                          
[5184] "Myself condemned and myself excus’d."                                                 
[5185] ""                                                                                     
[5186] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5187] "Then say at once what thou dost know in this."                                        
[5188] ""                                                                                     
[5189] "FRIAR LAWRENCE."                                                                      
[5190] "I will be brief, for my short date of breath"                                         
[5191] "Is not so long as is a tedious tale."                                                 
[5192] "Romeo, there dead, was husband to that Juliet,"                                       
[5193] "And she, there dead, that Romeo’s faithful wife."                                     
[5194] "I married them; and their stol’n marriage day"                                        
[5195] "Was Tybalt’s doomsday, whose untimely death"                                          
[5196] "Banish’d the new-made bridegroom from this city;"                                     
[5197] "For whom, and not for Tybalt, Juliet pin’d."                                          
[5198] "You, to remove that siege of grief from her,"                                         
[5199] "Betroth’d, and would have married her perforce"                                       
[5200] "To County Paris. Then comes she to me,"                                               
[5201] "And with wild looks, bid me devise some means"                                        
[5202] "To rid her from this second marriage,"                                                
[5203] "Or in my cell there would she kill herself."                                          
[5204] "Then gave I her, so tutored by my art,"                                               
[5205] "A sleeping potion, which so took effect"                                              
[5206] "As I intended, for it wrought on her"                                                 
[5207] "The form of death. Meantime I writ to Romeo"                                          
[5208] "That he should hither come as this dire night"                                        
[5209] "To help to take her from her borrow’d grave,"                                         
[5210] "Being the time the potion’s force should cease."                                      
[5211] "But he which bore my letter, Friar John,"                                             
[5212] "Was stay’d by accident; and yesternight"                                              
[5213] "Return’d my letter back. Then all alone"                                              
[5214] "At the prefixed hour of her waking"                                                   
[5215] "Came I to take her from her kindred’s vault,"                                         
[5216] "Meaning to keep her closely at my cell"                                               
[5217] "Till I conveniently could send to Romeo."                                             
[5218] "But when I came, some minute ere the time"                                            
[5219] "Of her awaking, here untimely lay"                                                    
[5220] "The noble Paris and true Romeo dead."                                                 
[5221] "She wakes; and I entreated her come forth"                                            
[5222] "And bear this work of heaven with patience."                                          
[5223] "But then a noise did scare me from the tomb;"                                         
[5224] "And she, too desperate, would not go with me,"                                        
[5225] "But, as it seems, did violence on herself."                                           
[5226] "All this I know; and to the marriage"                                                 
[5227] "Her Nurse is privy. And if ought in this"                                             
[5228] "Miscarried by my fault, let my old life"                                              
[5229] "Be sacrific’d, some hour before his time,"                                            
[5230] "Unto the rigour of severest law."                                                     
[5231] ""                                                                                     
[5232] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5233] "We still have known thee for a holy man."                                             
[5234] "Where’s Romeo’s man? What can he say to this?"                                        
[5235] ""                                                                                     
[5236] "BALTHASAR."                                                                           
[5237] "I brought my master news of Juliet’s death,"                                          
[5238] "And then in post he came from Mantua"                                                 
[5239] "To this same place, to this same monument."                                           
[5240] "This letter he early bid me give his father,"                                         
[5241] "And threaten’d me with death, going in the vault,"                                    
[5242] "If I departed not, and left him there."                                               
[5243] ""                                                                                     
[5244] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5245] "Give me the letter, I will look on it."                                               
[5246] "Where is the County’s Page that rais’d the watch?"                                    
[5247] "Sirrah, what made your master in this place?"                                         
[5248] ""                                                                                     
[5249] "PAGE."                                                                                
[5250] "He came with flowers to strew his lady’s grave,"                                      
[5251] "And bid me stand aloof, and so I did."                                                
[5252] "Anon comes one with light to ope the tomb,"                                           
[5253] "And by and by my master drew on him,"                                                 
[5254] "And then I ran away to call the watch."                                               
[5255] ""                                                                                     
[5256] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5257] "This letter doth make good the Friar’s words,"                                        
[5258] "Their course of love, the tidings of her death."                                      
[5259] "And here he writes that he did buy a poison"                                          
[5260] "Of a poor ’pothecary, and therewithal"                                                
[5261] "Came to this vault to die, and lie with Juliet."                                      
[5262] "Where be these enemies? Capulet, Montague,"                                           
[5263] "See what a scourge is laid upon your hate,"                                           
[5264] "That heaven finds means to kill your joys with love!"                                 
[5265] "And I, for winking at your discords too,"                                             
[5266] "Have lost a brace of kinsmen. All are punish’d."                                      
[5267] ""                                                                                     
[5268] "CAPULET."                                                                             
[5269] "O brother Montague, give me thy hand."                                                
[5270] "This is my daughter’s jointure, for no more"                                          
[5271] "Can I demand."                                                                        
[5272] ""                                                                                     
[5273] "MONTAGUE."                                                                            
[5274] "But I can give thee more,"                                                            
[5275] "For I will raise her statue in pure gold,"                                            
[5276] "That whiles Verona by that name is known,"                                            
[5277] "There shall no figure at such rate be set"                                            
[5278] "As that of true and faithful Juliet."                                                 
[5279] ""                                                                                     
[5280] "CAPULET."                                                                             
[5281] "As rich shall Romeo’s by his lady’s lie,"                                             
[5282] "Poor sacrifices of our enmity."                                                       
[5283] ""                                                                                     
[5284] "PRINCE."                                                                              
[5285] "A glooming peace this morning with it brings;"                                        
[5286] "The sun for sorrow will not show his head."                                           
[5287] "Go hence, to have more talk of these sad things."                                     
[5288] "Some shall be pardon’d, and some punished,"                                           
[5289] "For never was a story of more woe"                                                    
[5290] "Than this of Juliet and her Romeo."                                                   
[5291] ""                                                                                     
[5292] " [_Exeunt._]"

title: Text Analysis
text:
Tokens
A token is a meaningful unit of text, such as a word, that we are interested in using for analysis.

Examples:



Romeo
parting
[exit]
II
?



parting is (bi-gram)
parting is such (tri-gram)




In tidytext, use unnest_tokens(output, input, token = "words")

title: Text Analysis
text:

A two-dimensional data structure for atomic data. Created with matrix().

mat1

What does every row refer to, i.e. what is the unit of observation? What time range is covered by this data? How is prop calculated (what is the numerator and demoninator)?







In 2010, what proportion of boys names ended with a vowel? How about girls names? How does those proportions differ when calculated in 1910?







Narrow down the data frame to the rows with names that end in a diminuitive (e.g. “Joey” and “Juanita”). Do some research to gather a set of diminuitives used in languages found in American baby names.










How many distinct names rhyme with “Aiden”?







Create a plot like the following but for your name.



















Create a plot that shows the relatively frequency of a name shared by a historic figure over time (e.g. “Barack”).










Optional Challenge: For each year since 2000, which names have been the most gender neutral?








Optional Challenge: Plot the proportion of diminuitive names over time.









R has a built in palette of colors that you can access with colors(). Note that many of the colors in that palette have numbered variants that are different darknesses. How many colors are in this palette after removing the numbered variants of a color?







The following questions deal with the chorus of the song, “Golden”, but Huntrix. Be sure they copy into R as a string that captures the new line characters. Provide the code to programmatically answer each question. There are many ways to answer these questions but str_split() might be helpful.

\uc601\uc6d0\ud788 \uae68\uc9c8 \uc218 \uc5c6\ub294
Gonna be, gonna be golden"

How many times is the word "up” used in the chorus?






How many distinct four letter words are used?

section: How should we organize our cards into directories?
text:
How should we organize our cards into directories?
Boardwork.

Lead students into thinking about the information that we have on the other side of the card: Lab #, Years at Cal, and Stats Major (yes/no).
As they propose one form of sorting, say by years at Cal, ask them if we can do any sorting within each directory – in this case, by Stats Major.
Whichever sorting scheme they propose, draw it on the board as a tree with a root node (an empty circle), with lines leading to each of the top level directory (say, circles labelled “One”, “Two”, “Three”, and “Four”), and then for each, lines leading to circles of the subdirectories (“S” for stats major, “NS” for non-stats major, say), then with lines leading to the files. For those, tape the index cards in the appropriate place.

title: Data in Trees
section: How can we specify the location of a file/directory in the tree?
text:
How can we specify the location of a file/directory in the tree?


Path


A description of a file or directory’s location in the file system, written as a sequence of folder names that leads to it, separated by /.1
Absolute path: Starts from the root of the file system, indicated by /. Example: /Documents/Schoolwork/HW1.pdf



What absolute paths are found in our tree?

Return to the board and circle a file or two and ask for someone to provide you the absolute path. Write it on the board (be sure to start with /). Repeat by asking the path to a directory. Circle that directory and write the path next to it (it will start with a / and end with the name of that directory).


\ is used on older Windows computers but newer versions recognize the more standard /.

title: Data in Trees
text:
Path


A description of a file or directory’s location in the file system, written as a sequence of folder names that leads to it, separated by /.
Absolute path: Starts from the root of the file system, indicated by /. Example: /Documents/Schoolwork/HW1.pdf
Relative path: Starts from the current directory and shows how to reach a target. .. means “go up one level”. Example if you’re in Documents, Schoolwork/HW1.pdf



What relative paths are found in our tree?

On the board pick at least two relative paths for them to give you, one that goes from a directory to a file in a subdirectory, and another that requires going “up one level” to a file in a differet directory at the same level. You can indiated the “start” and “end” of the relative path using, say a square and a triangle.

title: Data in Trees
text:
UNIX1 Commands


pwd


Returns your present working directory.




ls


Lists the contents of your present working directory.


UNIX is a family of operating systems that includes Linux and MacOS. Most of the commands work on windows too.

title: Data in Trees
text:
cd


Changes your directory to the path provided (after a space). Examples:

cd Homework: (relative) only takes you into the Homework directory if you’re in Documents.
cd /Document/Homework: (absolute) takes you into the Homework directory regardless of your pwd.





cat


Prints to the screen the contents of the file at the path provided. Example: cat 127.txt.

Joins
A join is an operation that combines two data frames by linking the rows by their unique identifier called a key.

This can be done in six ways.

Right join
Full join
Inner join
Semi join
Anti join

An R vector for date-times

POSIXct (Portable Operating System Interface Calendar Time) is an atomic vector to store date-times that is built on top of a double vector.



now <- Sys.time()
now



[1] "2025-10-25 19:35:29 UTC"





class(now)



[1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt" 



Start off with reminder about factors: a integer vector with the factor class that allows it to store the levels look up table.

title: Dates and Times I
section: Why not just use a double vector?
text:
Why not just use a double vector?


# it prints as a legible string
now



[1] "2025-10-25 19:35:29 UTC"





# while respecting artithmetic
now + 1



[1] "2025-10-25 19:35:30 UTC"





# and other sensible operations
round(now)



[1] "2025-10-25 19:35:30 UTC"





# and makes it easy to use other formats
format(now, "%m/%d/%y")
